name: Old Cayman Sign Language
world_status: a description exists but is not accessible

earlier_scan.source_named: Sign language; only Washabaugh 1980/1981 classification refs on Glottolog; no description of the language located

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid pages oldc1248 (Old Cayman Sign Language) and prov1248 (Providencia-Cayman Sign, pseudo family). Hammarström, Forkel, Haspelmath & Bank (eds).
sources.note: Only references are Washabaugh 1980 and 1981, both cited for 'comments on subclassification'; zero descriptive references (grammar/phonology/sketch).

sources.citation: Webster, Jennifer & Josefina Safar. 2020. Ideologies behind the scoring of factors to rate sign language vitality. Language & Communication 74: 113-129 (author accepted manuscript). doi:10.1016/j.langcom.2020.06.003
sources.note: Nothing on stress or structure. One sentence (manuscript p. 21): 'Braithwaite (2019) notes that a signed language in Grand Cayman had already died out by the time it was described by Washabaugh (1981), and that though this is a well-known study in sign language linguistics, there are no follow-up studies.'

sources.citation: Wikipedia: Old Cayman Sign Language (stub) and Providence Island Sign Language.
sources.note: OCSL stub cites only Glottolog. Providencia SL page lists Washabaugh, Woodward & DeSantis 1978 (Anthropological Linguistics 20: 95-109), Woodward 1978, 1987, Meir et al. 2010; no phonology, prosody or stress content; no description of Old Cayman SL.

sources.citation: Washabaugh, William, James Woodward & Susan DeSantis. 1978. Providence Island Sign: A context-dependent language. Anthropological Linguistics 20(3): 95-109.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Earliest structural sketch of Providence Island Sign; relevant to the family only, not to Old Cayman SL directly.

sources.citation: Braithwaite, Ben. 2019. Sign language endangerment and linguistic diversity. Language 95(1): e161-e187.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Secondary: states (per Webster & Safar 2020) that the Grand Cayman signing had died out by the time Washabaugh described it and that no follow-up studies exist; useful for the identity/status note, not for stress.

sources.citation: Washabaugh, William. 1986. Five Fingers for Survival. Ann Arbor: Karoma Publishers.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: Book-length description of Providence Island Sign Language, the sister/descendant variety in Glottolog's Providencia-Cayman pseudo-family; may discuss the Cayman origin and the structure of the signing; the closest thing to a grammar for this family.

sources.citation: Washabaugh, William. 1981. The Deaf of Grand Cayman, British West Indies. Sign Language Studies 31: 117-134.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: The only first-hand description of the language known to Glottolog and the secondary literature; sociolinguistic in orientation, so at most it might contain remarks on the structure of the signing (a stress statement is unlikely). Opening it would settle whether any structural/prosodic remark exists.

sources.citation: Kusters, Annelies. 2010. Deaf utopias? Reviewing the sociocultural literature on the world's 'Martha's Vineyard situations'. Journal of Deaf Studies and Deaf Education 15(1): 3-16. doi:10.1093/deafed/enp026
